CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1

CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1 · SEPTEMBER

Lines in space

On the air traffic control map two flight paths cross. Will the planes collide? Not necessarily: in space, lines can pass each other as skew lines. You learn to describe lines with a parametric equation, to check whether a point lies on them, and to decide for two lines how they are positioned relative to each other.

8 LESSONS2 UNITSREAL 3DAVIATION
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • give lines in point-direction form and two-point form
  • use the point test to check whether a point lies on a line, and calculate trace points
  • determine the relative position of two lines: identical, parallel, intersecting or skew
  • calculate the point of intersection and the angle of intersection

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Equations of lines and the point test

The laser is at $P(0, 0, 1)$, the beam goes in the direction $\vec{u} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0.5 \\ 0.25 \end{pmatrix}$. After $t$ steps the spot of light is at $X(t, 0.5t, 1 + 0.25t)$. It reaches the wall $x = 8$ for $t = 8$, at the point $(8, 4, 3)$. A single number $t$, the parameter, describes every point of the beam.

Every line in space is determined by a point and a direction. You start from the position point and attach any multiples of the direction vector. If you know two points $A$ and $B$, you take $A$ as the position point and $\vec{AB}$ as the direction.

KEY POINT · PARAMETRIC EQUATION OF A LINE

Point-direction form: $g\colon \vec{x} = \vec{p} + t \cdot \vec{u}$ with $t \in \mathbb{R}$, position vector $\vec{p}$, direction vector $\vec{u} \neq \vec{0}$

Two-point form: $g\colon \vec{x} = \vec{OA} + t \cdot \vec{AB}$. The line segment $AB$ belongs to $0 \le t \le 1$.

Point test: substitute $Q$, solve every row for $t$. The same $t$ in all three rows: $Q \in g$, otherwise $Q \notin g$.

Trace points are the points of intersection with the coordinate planes: for $S_{xy}$ you set $z = 0$, for $S_{xz}$ $y = 0$, for $S_{yz}$ $x = 0$.

Many equations, one line: every point of the line will do as the position point, every multiple $r \cdot \vec{u}$ with $r \neq 0$ as the direction.

Watch out for zeros: if a row of the direction vector is zero, the coordinate of $Q$ there must match the position point exactly.

INTERACTIVE · A LINE IN SPACE

The slider moves the point $X$ along the line. The red points are the trace points. Enter coordinates of your own for $Q$ and read off the point test.

EXAMPLE 1 · TWO POINTS AND A TEST

Set up an equation of the line through $A(2, -1, 3)$ and $B(4, 3, -1)$. Do $C(5, 5, -3)$ and $D(3, 1, 2)$ lie on it?

$g\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$

$C$: $t = \tfrac32$ in all rows, so $C \in g$ (beyond $B$). $D$: $t = \tfrac12,\ \tfrac12,\ \tfrac14$, so $D \notin g$.

EXAMPLE 2 · TRACE POINTS

Calculate the trace points of $g\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, the line in the widget.

$z = 0$: $1 + 2t = 0$, $t = -\tfrac12$, so $S_{xy}(0.5, 2.5, 0)$.

$y = 0$: $t = 2$, $S_{xz}(3, 0, 5)$ · $x = 0$: $t = -1$, $S_{yz}(0, 3, -1)$

EXERCISES

Give an equation of the line through $A(1, 0, 2)$ and $B(3, 4, 1)$. Then give a second equation of the same line.

$\vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, for example also $\vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + s \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ -8 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$

Check whether $P(5, -1, 6)$ and $Q(3, 0, 4)$ lie on $g\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

$P$: $t = 2$ three times, $P \in g$. $Q$: $t = 1,\ 1,\ \tfrac43$, $Q \notin g$.

For which number $a$ does $R(7, a, 9)$ lie on the line $g$ from exercise 2?

The first and the third row determine $t$.

$1 + 2t = 7$ and $3t = 9$ both give $t = 3$, then $a = 1 - 3 = -2$.

Calculate the trace points of $h\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$.

$S_{xy}(4, 3, 0)$ for $t = 2$, $S_{xz}(1, 0, 6)$ for $t = -1$, $S_{yz}(0, -1, 8)$ for $t = -2$

A plane takes off at the origin (values in km) and climbs in a straight line. After one minute it is at $B(3, 4, 0.5)$. How high is it above the place with the map coordinates $(12, 16)$? When does it reach an altitude of 10 km, and how fast is it flying?

$\vec{x} = t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$, $t$ in minutes. Above $(12, 16)$, $t = 4$: 2 km high. 10 km after $t = 20$ minutes. Per minute $\sqrt{25.25} \approx 5.02$ km, about 301 km/h.

TEST YOURSELF!

For which $t$ does $\vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ give the point $(7, 2, 0)$?

$t = 3$

What is the $x$-coordinate of the trace point $S_{xy}$ of $\vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$?

$z = 0$ for $t = 2$: $S_{xy}(3, 5, 0)$

Which vector is a direction vector of the line through $A(1, 2, 3)$ and $B(3, 3, 1)$?

$\vec{AB} = (2, 1, -2)$, times $-2$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Relative positions, point of intersection and angle of intersection

Flight A: $\vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 10 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, flight B: $\vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 12 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix} + s \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \\ 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$. From $x$ and $y$ it follows that $t = s = 2$; both are then above $(8, 6)$. But the altitudes are 10 km and 7 km: the third equation is false, the paths do not intersect.

First you compare the direction vectors. If they are collinear, the lines are parallel, perhaps even identical. If they are not, you set the equations equal. That gives three equations for the two unknowns $t$ and $s$: you solve two of them, and the third decides.

KEY POINT · POSITION OF TWO LINES

Direction vectors collinear: the position point of $h$ lies on $g$ → identical, otherwise strictly parallel.

Not collinear: solve $\vec{p} + t\vec{u} = \vec{q} + s\vec{v}$. One solution → intersecting (substitute to get the point of intersection), no solution → skew.

Angle of intersection: $\cos \varphi = \dfrac{|\vec{u} \circ \vec{v}|}{|\vec{u}| \cdot |\vec{v}|}$, $0^\circ \le \varphi \le 90^\circ$ · orthogonal if $\vec{u} \circ \vec{v} = 0$

Only in space: skew lines do not exist in the plane. There two lines always intersect if they are not parallel.

With the graphing calculator: let it solve two rows as a system of linear equations, check the third row by hand.

INTERACTIVE · TWO LINES

Choose an example or enter position points and directions of your own. For skew lines the red line segment shows the shortest distance.

EXAMPLE 3 · POINT OF INTERSECTION AND ANGLE

$g\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $h\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} + s \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$

Not collinear. $1 + t = 1 + s$ and $2t = 3 - s$ give $t = s = 1$. Third row: $2 - 1 = -1 + 2$ ✔ $S(2, 2, 1)$

$\cos \varphi = \dfrac{|1 - 2 - 2|}{\sqrt6 \cdot \sqrt6} = \tfrac12$: $\varphi = 60^\circ$

EXAMPLE 4 · PARALLEL OR IDENTICAL?

$g\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$, $h\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix} + s \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ 2 \\ -6 \end{pmatrix}$

$\vec{v} = -2\vec{u}$: parallel. Point test of $(5, 0, 6)$ in $g$: $t = 2$ in all rows.

identical. With the position point $(5, 0, 7)$ they would be strictly parallel.

EXERCISES

Are the direction vectors collinear? a) $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ -6 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$   b) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$

a) yes, factor $-3$   b) no

Find the point of intersection and the angle of intersection of $g\colon \vec{x} = t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $h\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + s \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

$t = 2 - s$ and $t = s$: $s = t = 1$, $S(1, 1, 1)$. $\cos \varphi = \tfrac13$, $\varphi \approx 70.5^\circ$.

Investigate the relative position of $g\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $h\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + s \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Not collinear. First row $t = 2$, second $s = -1$, third: $1 + 4 = 5 \neq -1$: skew.

Find $a$ such that $g\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $h\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \\ a \end{pmatrix} + s \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ intersect.

The second row gives $t$, then the first gives $s$.

$t = 3$, $s = 1 + t = 4$, third row $0 = a + 4$: $a = -4$, point of intersection $S(4, 3, 0)$.

In a factory hall two pipes run along $g\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $h\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + s \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0.2 \end{pmatrix}$ (in m). Show that they do not meet. How far apart vertically are they at the place where they cross in the floor plan?

From $x$ and $y$: $t = 4$, $s = 8$. Heights: $g$ 3 m, $h$ $1 + 1.6 = 2.6$ m. The third row does not match: skew. Above the point $(4, 8)$, $g$ lies 40 cm above $h$.

TEST YOURSELF!

$g\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $h\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + s \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$. What is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection?

$t = s = 2$: $S(4, 2, 1)$

What is the angle of intersection of lines with the directions $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$?

Scalar product $0$: $90^\circ$

The direction vectors are not collinear, the system of equations has no solution. The lines are …

Not parallel and no common point.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Give two points of the line $\vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$. Why does every one of its points have the $x$-coordinate 3?

For example $(3, -1, 2)$ and $(3, 1, 7)$. The first row of the direction vector is zero: the line lies in the plane $x = 3$.

Connecting with chapter 1.1: a cube with edge 2 has one vertex at the origin. Show that the space diagonals from $(0, 0, 0)$ to $(2, 2, 2)$ and from $(2, 0, 0)$ to $(0, 2, 2)$ intersect at the centre of the cube.

$t \cdot (2, 2, 2) = (2, 0, 0) + s \cdot (-2, 2, 2)$: $2t = 2s$ and $2t = 2 - 2s$, so $t = s = \tfrac12$, point of intersection $(1, 1, 1)$.

For $g\colon \vec{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + t \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ give a strictly parallel line, an intersecting line and a skew line.

Parallel: $\vec{x} = s \cdot (1, 0, -1)$. Intersecting: $\vec{x} = (1, 2, 3) + s \cdot (0, 1, 0)$. Skew: $\vec{x} = s \cdot (0, 1, 0)$, because $1 + t = 0$ requires $t = -1$, and then $z = 4 \neq 0$.

Use the equations from the starter of unit 2 to show that flight A and flight B are skew. What is the difference in altitude above the crossing point on the map? Compare it with the required minimum separation from the excursion.

Directions $(4, 3, 0)$ and $(4, -3, 0.5)$ not collinear, $t = s = 2$ violates the third row: skew. Above $(8, 6)$ 10 km against 7 km, so 3 km, far more than 300 m.

EXCURSIONAVIATION

A thousand feet apart

Thousands of aircraft are in the air over Europe at the same time. Air traffic control makes sure that no two of them come too close. Between the flight levels FL 290 and FL 410, that is between about 8.8 km and 12.5 km altitude, aircraft flying one above the other must keep at least 1000 feet, about 300 m, apart. Side by side, radar control usually requires 5 nautical miles, a good 9 km.

For every pair of flight paths the controllers’ systems calculate in advance whether the paths intersect or are skew, and how close they come. Exactly the calculation from this chapter, only with time and the curvature of the Earth added.

Source: ICAO Doc 9574, “Manual on Implementation of a 300 m (1 000 ft) Vertical Separation Minimum Between FL 290 and FL 410 Inclusive”; 5 NM radar separation according to ICAO Doc 4444 (PANS-ATM). Overview: SKYbrary, “Separation Standards”.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

EQUATION OF A LINE

$\vec{x} = \vec{p} + t \cdot \vec{u}$, through two points with $\vec{u} = \vec{AB}$

$A(2, -1, 3)$, $B(4, 3, -1)$: $\vec{u} = (2, 4, -4)$

POINT TEST

Solve every row for $t$; the same $t$ means: the point lies on the line.

$C(5, 5, -3)$: $t = 1.5$ three times

TRACE POINTS

Set one coordinate to zero.

$z = 0$ gives $S_{xy}$

POSITION

Collinear: identical or parallel. Otherwise set equal: intersecting or skew.

Three equations, two unknowns: the third decides.

ANGLE OF INTERSECTION

$\cos \varphi = \dfrac{|\vec{u} \circ \vec{v}|}{|\vec{u}|\,|\vec{v}|}$

$(1, 2, -1)$, $(1, -1, 2)$: $60^\circ$
